utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. From the office of the Prosecutor, Gerard Dobbyn with senior trial attorney Joanna Korner, Crispian Smith, and today we have the assistance of one of our interns, Catherine Loftus.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Mico Stanisic's [Realtime transcript read in error "Stojan Zupljanin"] Defence team, Slobodan Cvijetic and Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, can I raise the question or come back to the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, just one thing for the record. It's Monday, so we are not starting as we should. It should say that we are the Defence for Mico Stanisic, not Stojan Zupljanin as the record indicates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's passed me by completely, but anyhow can I go back to where I was. Your Honours, Your Honours raised the question of timings last Friday, and said you would be returning to it this morning. Your Honours, we've, with a great deal of difficulty, attempted to work out where we are on timings and the various additions that had been given us. The total provided by the Registry on Friday was that the Prosecution team had spent a total of 253 hours, 14 minutes in examination-in-chief, and we think that is probably right, give or take a few minutes here or there. Your Honours, the original hours you gave us was 212, when we had asked for 292 for the original witnesses. The Registry's examination-in-chief total includes, of course, some of the new witnesses which have been added for which we were given extra time, and for the life of us, with -- and we did have Ms. Loftus attempting to do her best to work out how this was all fitting, and we can't do it, it's just too complicated, as far as we're concerned, unless you've managed to do it, which I'm sure you have, particularly Judge Delvoie, but Your Honours, can I make this point: Of the original witnesses who are left, there are only three of them; that is to say, ST-004, ST-190, and Mr. Brown, who I think is ST-097. So had it not been for the various to-ings and fro-ings and dropping and adding of witnesses, we would have come in certainly to finish this week. But Your Honours, what I want to say is this: We will come in within that original total that we added up, and which we knew our case at the time we gave it, or thought we knew our case until the question of the adjudicated facts came up. And we gave a pretty realistic estimate of what it would take. Your Honours, we would say this: That the -- that the -- that the 212 you gave us was before the case started, when nobody knew really what the issues were, as we've raised a number of times, the Defence's pre-trial brief didn't exactly assist very much. Nobody knew how difficult some of the witnesses were going to be, in particular, the -- the difficulty in getting them to answer questions. And, accordingly, without going into further nuts and bolts about how many hours we actually have left and what comes from the new witnesses and what doesn't, we would simply ask that Your Honours allow us to complete the evidence that we have got left within the hours we've asked for for each of those witnesses. Your Honour, we -- we -- we sincerely believe that you wouldn't wish to cut off what is clearly relevant evidence in this case because we have actually run over the hours. Your Honour, the second matter is this: The witness that Mr. Dobbyn is about to call, Your Honours announced although we asked for two hours, or two and a bit hours, I think, that we were limited to an hour, and I think it's best if Mr. Dobbyn explains to you why it is going to be very difficult to get him through in one hour. Your Honours, those are the submissions we make which effectively can be summed up this way: We simply ask for sufficient time to complete the evidence that we have applied for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it seems that, as far as the number of witnesses you have left, the three that you mention do not include today's and tomorrow's witnesses, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So that is altogether five witnesses that you think you have left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of the very original list, sir, the 65 ter list, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But then other witnesses have been added in the course of the trial --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Other witnesses have been added and you have given us more time for those witnesses. That's why I say it became incredibly complicated trying to work out the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But as of this moment at least five witnesses remain to be heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, many more, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Not including the adjudicated fact witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it may be more. I'd have to go back and have another check. There are these two witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And then three more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And three more from the original list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So that is at least five and we think that there are a couple of more witnesses on top of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In any case, today's witness, 221, I think was given half an hour. He is 92 ter and we allowed an extra 10 minutes to show the video to him, as was claimed, so for this witness today there is 30 minutes for the Prosecution's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I say, it's the one following that's -- that may be the problem. Who may start today in any event. He is here. The only matter that concerns him is the Defence have asked to speak to him this morning, as a result of the something he told the Prosecution during the course of the proofing session. And that's the only thing that may cause a delay. Your Honour, the only reason I'm raising all this is because it was raised by Your Honours on Friday. But, as I say, all we can do is say that we would like sufficient time to call the witnesses already granted, plus, if Your Honours are minded to grant it, the extra two that we asked for last week. And I think there may be some -- actually, I'm not sure Your Honours have rendered a decision on some of the other witnesses. Can I add one final thing. There is actually no question in our mind that, bar the witness Mr. Brown, and potentially the other two witnesses we've applied for, we will be finishing our case in very early December. We -- we -- we worked that one out; subject, of course, to the Defence not changing their estimates on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, did Mr. Dobbyn wish to be heard now on this question of the time for the following witness? Or he would reserve that until the witness is about to be called?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to address that now. It may be easier so that both Prosecution and Defence know what will be happening for the following witness. And Your Honours, that witness, when we sought to add him along with the witness who is about to come in, we had sought that -- well, we had indicated when seeking to add him to the 65 ter list that we would be looking to call him 92 ter with an additional one hour of direct. However, upon speaking to the witness, we realize that it wouldn't be suitable to call him 92 ter, just simply wasn't feasible under the circumstances. Now this witness speaks about -- the reason it wouldn't have been feasible, Your Honours, was that he was not happy with the statement he given to the Office of the Prosecutor. He claimed there were many inaccuracies in there, so under those circumstances we felt we couldn't put that statement and just have him speak to additional matters beyond that for that one hour. So we're in the position now where we can't use the statement that he given us. He will be giving evidence on four detention facilities in Zvornik, and he is in unique position to give very relevant and useful information about those detention facilities. On top of that, there are several documents, also a video which will be shown to him. He is also a witness who is in a position to clear up some confusion that I understand was remaining from the site visit as to the physical location and appearances of some of these detention facilities. So under these circumstances, particularly looking at four different detention facilities, an hour viva voce simply -- I don't see how it would be possible to get through that evidence in that time, which is why we indicated we were hoping to have two and a half hours with him. Two hours may be possible with this witness to get him through that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify with the OTP, will the witness remain 92 ter or is he going to be viva voce? I didn't understand, are they just asking for additional time, to which have I no objection. I just want to clarify the status of the witness. I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I'm talking about the next witness, not today's witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm talking about ST-222, and that's the one that we'll be seeking to call viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And Your Honours, he is currently listed for tomorrow but the indications are that the witness we have coming in next will be finished before the end of the day so he may actually be in a position to be starting today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Provided, if I understand you correctly, the Defence is through with their speaking with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes. And the communications I've had is that they were only looking for approximately half an hour to speak to him relating to a matter that arose out of proofing. He is being brought over at 10.30 so we should be able to go straight on to that witness, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the Defence for Zupljanin have a view on this, the extended time sought for in respect of 222?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not have any position regarding this, because this refers mainly Mr. Stanisic Defence witnesses. Therefore, we concur with what his Defence team has stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we would let you know where we stand on this obviously before the witness takes the stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so the blinds to be lowered so that the next witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you read the solemn declaration, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I trust that you are hearing me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the solemn declaration that you have just taken imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony, and the penalty for giving untruthful or misleading testimony is the -- lies in the powers that this Tribunal has to impose penalties for perjury, which the Statute creating this Tribunal empowers it to impose. You have, for reasons peculiar to yourself, been granted the ability to have your testimony received with certain protective measures namely, that, whereas, the -- it is not a closed session in the sense that persons outside of this hearing room would not be able to hear what you were saying. They would not be able to identify you either by voice or by your face because both your voice and image are distorted in terms of any broadcast, and have been granted a pseudonym. And all of these are measures that would not allow anyone outside of the hearing room to identify you as the person who is giving testimony. And I would, first of all, ask the Prosecution if they have a pseudonym sheet prepared, to have the usher hand it to you, and if you are satisfied that it correctly identifies you and your -- gives your date of birth, you would sign it and hand it back to the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And that would be admitted under seal and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P01690, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Witness, and I will refer to you as such to avoid accidentally revealing your identity, you have been called under an expedited procedure whereby the Prosecution would only spend about 30 minutes in examining you in-chief and the Defence for the first accused has indicated that their cross-examination of you may last for approximately three hours. The day's sitting of the Tribunal, which ends at 1.45 in order to make the courtroom available for another trial, is divided into intervals of no more than 90 minutes, which allows the tapes which record the proceedings to be changed and also allows for the comfort of yourself and counsel and -- and everyone else involved in the trial. But notwithstanding those set breaks, if at any other point you need to take a break, if you indicate it to us, we will, of course, accommodate you. If we may go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 17th and 18th of May, 2003?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes. I provided a statement on the 17th and 18th of March [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was this statement read back to you in your own language, and did you then sign it as being true and correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the statement. The interpreter who was in Berlin had read it to me. She was there together with a lady from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall meeting with me and with an investigator from the OTP on the 6th of October, 2010, just over a month ago?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I remember that you were in Berlin on the 6th of October. I had a meeting with you, with an investigator, and with an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: On that occasion, sir, did you review your statement and did you make some corrections to that statement in the form of a declaration?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed the statement. I did have a few objections. We made some corrections, and we drafted a declaration to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And are you satisfied that the content of your statement, with the corrections contained in the declaration, is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I made all the corrections, and I believe that now my statement is fully accurate. Everything in it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So, sir, is the information contained in your statement and the declaration the same as you would give if testifying in full today?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I would provide the same information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement and the declaration have the 65 ter numbers 9119 and 10576 and I'll seek to tender those, I believe, at the end of this witness's testimony. Now, at this point, Your Honours, I'd like to read a brief summary of his evidence. Because of his particular position it's difficult to do so in much detail without giving away his identity. What I propose to do, if Your Honours would like, is that we go into private session and I read a short summary for Your Honours' benefit and then a much shorter summary again for the public's benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In his 92 ter statement, ST-221 describes events in Zvornik in 1992. Throughout the indictment period until August 1992 ST-221 lived and worked in Zvornik. Up until leaving Zvornik in August 1992, ST-221 became aware of the existence of a number of detention facilities in Zvornik where non-Serbs were held and he also gained some knowledge of the numbers of non-Serbs dead in Zvornik and its surrounds. ST-221 has knowledge of an occasion in June 1992 when Muslims were driven to Gero slaughter-house where they were taken inside and executed by paramilitaries. The witness also has specific knowledge concerning the killing of a large number of Muslims at Drinjaca school on or about 30 May, 1992. And that concludes the summary, Your Honours. I now have some questions to expand and clarify some issues contained in there. First of all, if we could show 65 ter 10236.16. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, if we could perhaps just scroll up to the top to start with. And, sir, what you'll see on the screen in front of you is a map showing the ethnic composition and distribution of Zvornik municipality in 1991. You'll see that Serbs are denoted by blue; Croats by red; and Muslims by green. In the numbers in the table at the top, it shows that in 1991 approximately 60 per cent of the position of Zvornik was Muslim; approximately 35 per cent was Serb; and the remainder was split between Croats, others, and those who described themselves as Yugoslavs. Sir, from your knowledge of living in Zvornik in 1991, are those figures correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The figures are correct. There may have been a few more Muslims, but the 60 per cent or 68 per cent of Muslims resided in the territory of Zvornik. The rest were Serbs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could scroll down to show the map itself. And, sir, on the map, you'll see that settlements are shown. Those in green are those that had a majority Muslim population; those in blue those with the majority Serb population. And, again, from your personal knowledge, does that distribution seem accurate for 1991?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Zvornik is marked with green. There is Celopek next to it. Trsic, Dabanci, and all the way to Kozluk the villages were mostly Serbs. You can see that all of those villages are blue. I used to travel that route quite often, and Bileca, as you see it, everything that you see in the map reflects the situation as it was at the time in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this map at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01691. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in paragraph 10 of your statement, you describe the start of the war in Zvornik in early April and then shelling and an attack on Kula Grad. And when you say that Kula Grad was being shelled and was then attacked, which side or which group was this that was doing the shelling and then launched this attack?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: When we fled to Kula Grad, shelling started in the evening, and the shelling was carried out by the tank unit from the town of Zvornik below us. There were tanks deployed there and from there Kula Grad was shelled. During the night, they did not launch proper shells, only in the morning at 5.00 the shelling started with live shells. People started dying and then people started fleeing towards Tuzla. I was among them, together with my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, sire, when you say that there were tanks performing the shelling and they launched the attack, again, just to be precise, which group was this, which -- which organ or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: They were Serbs, and the tanks belonged to the JNA. At that time the VRS did not exist. They were billeted in Celopek. The commander of that unit was Jovanovic. I don't know his first name. He was the commander of that tank unit. In other words, the attack was launched by the JNA and by the Serbs. They attacked those people up there in Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you also describe bodies of 100 to 120 people that you assumed were interrogated and killed by paramilitaries in the Alhos factory in Karakaj and were then buried in the Kazanbasca cemetery. Now, at this time, which you put at late April, was there any police presence in or around Alhos factory and the industrial area?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: There were police there, but whatever was done was done by paramilitaries, and those paramilitaries had come from Serbia. They called themselves Zuca, Pivarski, Crni, Niski. The proper police only issued passes and they were not involved in anything else. Nobody asked them anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now these 100 to 120 people that were killed, what ethnicity were the victims; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: They were Muslims, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you see how they were dressed? If so, did you see if they were in uniforms or in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The Muslims who were killed all wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the next series of questions, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraph 43 of your statement, you say that you had a friend who was detained at Ekonomija farm and was never seen again. Do you remember your friend's name?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: His name was Mensur Salihovic, also known as Meco [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, did you ever hear of any building referred to as Ekonomija factory?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of Ekonomija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And is this located where Ekonomija farm is?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Ekonomija is a -- the farm. It's not a factory. It's a farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd now look to call up 65 ter 2289.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: That's the Ekonomija farm. And that's the building at the farm, within the Ekonomija complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, do we have a tab number for this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] this is tab 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab 4. Oh. I'm missing tab 4. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, again, using the pen, could you draw a circle around the building it was that detainees were held in?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: A circle or a cross? What do you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If you could put a circle around it, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this photograph now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01693, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, and, please, if we could go back into private session for the next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you referred to prisoners being held at Celopek Dom Kulture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now 65 ter 2286.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes. That's the cultural centre in Celopek and people were imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd seek to tender this photo, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01695, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, next, I would like to call up 65 ter 2826. Could we please just go to page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, sir, if you look at the document in front of you, you'll see that it's -- purports to be a list of prisoners. Now at numbers 4 to 22, and also number 24, there are a number of people listed who are apparently from the town of Divic. Now, you've looked at this document before, and did you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I knew most of them. I know most of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know if they were detained in 1992, and, if so, at which detention facility?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Most of the people who were imprisoned were from Divic and they were mainly held at the cultural centre in Celopek. I saw them there. I saw them until Repic committed his crime and killed them. And then they closed down Celopek and they moved up to the building of Novi Izvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to have this document marked for identification at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 2826 shall be marked for identification as P01696. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, you asked for it to be marked. This is pending what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The following witness will speak about this and I think he is in a better position to have it tendered through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, I didn't catch the provenance of the documents when you showed page 1. Could you just tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a -- a list of -- actually, three separate lists of prisoners, and it was obtained, it was handed to the Office of the Prosecutor by a witness, a member of the RS MUP who has actually already testified in this case but it seems this particular document wasn't shown through that witness. A member of the, as I say, the RS MUP who had the three lists handed to him by the police in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. From what I was just able to pick up when we had a very brief look at page 1 was that it's a letter to Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic from who, exactly? And what was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, as far as the initial -- this cover page, this letter, that's something that I'm not sure that we know exactly who it comes from. Again, this letter was part of the list of prisoners. They were all handed over together to the OTP by this other witness who was member of the MUP, but as to who actually drafted this letter or where it originated from, I can't say at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, the last thing I'd like to do, sir, is to have you look at a video, and this is P908. And I'd like to start this video at 19 minutes and 37 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could play until 19 minutes and 43 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise anybody that you see on the screen at the moment?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: His last name is Srabovic. I don't know his first name, I'd forgotten it. I know the man very well but I have forgotten his first name. I know his last name was Srabovic, he was born in Tuzla and he lived and worked in Zvornika Glinica, down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And which individual are you referring to? Could you describe an item of clothing he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: He is in civilian clothing. He is the one that's wearing civilian clothing, and he's facing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know -- well, first of all, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. These were all Muslims who were fleeing Zvornik and were trying to get to Serbia across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know if he has ever returned to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I don't think he returned to Zvornik, because his wife worked together with me at the company and I think they're somewhere up north in Denmark or Sweden. I have not seen him since the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, if we could continue playing and stop next at 19 minutes and 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recognise anybody on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I recognise the man. His last name was Taljic, and I have forgotten his first name. He worked at Glinica; he was a lawyer. It's the same case as Srabovic; he was trying to get to Serbia and save his life. They were being searched. Some people lost their money or gold. These were all Muslims who were trying to flee to Serbia for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we could keep on playing now. And next stop will be at 20 minutes and 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] sorry, if you could keep on playing. Stop there, please. This is at 20 minutes and 55 seconds on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the man who was being led out of the building by the uniformed individual?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I recognise him. He was a municipal judge, Muhamed Zaimovic, and in the image he is in civilian clothing. I have no idea who the man wearing the uniform is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know if Muhamed Zaimovic --

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Muhamed Zaimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, and has he ever returned to Zvornik, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: No, I have never seen Muhamed Zaimovic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could continue playing, and the next stop will be at 21 minutes and 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: This at 21 minutes and 41 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise any of those individuals carrying the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I know these people. One was the leader of the team who was collecting the bodies. His name was Milan. I can't now recall his last name. These were his colleagues from Inzinjering, and, yes his name is Milan Radovic. His nickname was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the nickname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was collecting bodies. And these were two of his colleagues from the Inzjnjering Construction Company. I know these two men as well. I don't know their names. They were people with intellectual disabilities. It's impossible that a sane person would have been doing this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of questions. You had mentioned Milan Radovic's nickname but that wasn't caught by the interpreter. Could you say that again, please?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Milan Radovic, also known as Gluvac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And which of the individuals -- we see three men on the screen. Which of the three is Milan Radovic?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Milan Radovic is the one wearing the fur coat, with his back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could keep on playing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: For the record, we've stopped at 22 minutes and 28 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And sir, we can see people walking along the road. Do you know what's going on at this point?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: These were refugees from Zvornik and the neighbouring villages. They were fleeing towards Kula Grad and trying to get to Tuzla and the free territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what ethnicity were these refugees who were fleeing the town?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: They were all Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And there's just a few seconds to go. If we could continue playing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If could you stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recognise anybody in this clip? This is at 22 and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The man in the front is Ramiz Osmanovic. He worked at the public utilities company together with me. He fled to Tuzla and then he went to Germany, and currently he lives in the USA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, I have finished with the video-clip. I actually have forgotten I have two maps to finish up with which should just take a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. Could we go back in this video to the first two stops. I would like you to ask the witness about the uniformed man we see there, about the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Certainly. The first stop was at 19 minutes and 43 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir you see a man on the screen in front of you in a uniform. Do you know what uniform that is or which organ or organisation this person belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The one that's searching the man is a policeman. He has got a blue uniform on, and then he has got a flakjacket on top. He was from the Zvornik MUP. I don't know whether this might have been the Serbian side. There was police on the Bosnian side and on the Serbian side, and people were searched only on the Bosnian side and would then cross on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Any further questions, Your Honour, on that? The next stop was at 19 minutes and 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And sir, again here we see on the right-hand side of the screen a man in what looks like a blue beret and a flakjacket. Do you know which organ this person was from?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Again he was from the MUP, from the Zvornik MUP, except that he had a flakjacket on top. But his uniform was blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So we've finished with the video now. I'd like to call up 65 ter 3680.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen in front of you, you'll see a map of the industrial area of Zvornik. Now, from -- you have seen this map before. You were shown it on Saturday. Can you tell me if this is an accurate representation of the industrial area of Zvornik - Karakaj, that is - in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Just a moment for me to take a look. Yes. Yes, it's an accurate map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd ask for the usher's assistance now. I'd like you, first of all, to the far right of the map, you'll see the -- the settlement or the area of Celopek. And just underneath the road a building marked as the Dom. Now, is that, according to your recollection, the correct location of Celopek Dom Kulture; and, if so, could you put a circle around that.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes. That's the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you put a number 1 above that circle, please. Sorry, sir, could you put the number 1 above the circle that you've just marked.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And next to the left and down of that, you'll see Ekonomija marked. Now, is that the Ekonomija farm; and, if so, could you put a circle around that cluster of buildings.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Ekonomija. The number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, on this map, are you able to locate Gero's slaughter-house?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, please, with the number 3 on top.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, finally, sir, can you locate Karakaj Technical School on this map?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: That's the technical school. That's the technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now I see you've put a marking above that. Is that the number 4?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: It's the number 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd seek to tender this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01697, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Finally, I have one more map. And this is 65 ter 3681.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, what we have in front of us is somewhat difficult to see at this size, but it's a larger map of Zvornik, including the portion that we've just looked at in a separate map. Now, could we perhaps zoom in on this. And if we could scroll along so -- to the left, please. Now, sir, there is quite difficult to see at this size --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we go a bit further to the right. Thank you. That's good. Sorry, just a little bit more now to the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you -- can you locate Kula Grad on this map, which is one of the locations that you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Kula Grad is here, I can see it, yes. Shall I circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, please. Sorry, before marking it, could we just pull back a bit because we'll need to make another marking on the map as well.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I saw Kula Grad on the map. Shall I circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Not just yet. We're just waiting to get it to the right size. Thank you. That's fine there. Do you see Kula Grad now?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you circle it, please; and put the number 1 above that?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, finally, sir, do you -- are you able to locate on this map the SUP compound with -- the SUP building in Zvornik town, the basic court, and the municipal building? Do you know where that's located?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I can see it all here. It's all in one complex over there. I'll circle -- shall I circle them one by one or all together?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If you could just circle them all together with the number 2 on top, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this map with the markings and also the original without the markings as it included the whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the original of this map without the markings, which is 65 ter 3681, shall be given exhibit number 1698; while the marked version shall be given exhibit number P01699. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we are actually beyond the point at which we would ordinarily break, so before Mr. Cvijetic begins his cross-examination, we would take the break now and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: While the witness is brought in, Mr. Dobbyn, for the next one, that's ST-222; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is granting two hours for your examination. And we will add the difference between the 92 ter and the viva voce estimate to the total amount of hours Prosecutor is entitled to. So that -- that makes one hour and 30 minutes in addition. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness, can I just say something else. Your Honours, the Defence for Stanisic applied for provisional release over the Christmas break again. Can I, just so that it's all dealt with, say that the Prosecution takes no position on this and will leave it to the Trial Chamber. If that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- I'm sorry. Your Honours, I'm not going to ask your permission to begin, because I don't intend to begin at all. I presented my position to Mr. Stanisic, he approved it, and we consequently have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. And, Mr. Krgovic, I presume your position remains as indicated previously, that you have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this morning, when you were explaining what the Muslim people were trying to do, get to Serbia, across the bridge, if I'm right. And you also said they were trying to get to the free territories. Can I ask you what you mean by "free territories"? Not indicate where they were, but why are you calling them "free territories"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The free territories was something, to my understanding, the territories populated mainly by the Muslims, such as Kalesija in the direction of Tuzla. And from the town of Zvornik, whoever managed to get to Serbia, travelled further on via Serbia to Hungary and the third country. So one group of people sought salvation by fleeing to Serbia and the others sought salvation in the Muslim territories where they thought would be safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is on. Okay? I understand that, Mr. Witness, but what strikes me is that you, as a Serb, referred to those territories as "free territories," which supposes that Zvornik was not free. I mean, there's something I have difficulties to understand -- have difficulty to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The town of Zvornik was not free, as far as the Muslims were concerned. Because you can see from my statement that there were camps set up, people were being killed, people were afraid, and, therefore, they tried to flee where they would be free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now I understand. What you mean is free from the Muslim point of view. So that's -- that's clear now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we thank you, sir, for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released, and we wish a safe journey back to your home. The blinds could be lowered so the witness could be escorted from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, I assume the Prosecution is ready with its next witness immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you, sir, read the solemn declaration on the card that's just been handed to you. Actually, I suppose before he does that, the blinds should be raised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated. And I take it that you are hearing me in a language that you understand, from your responses so far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, first of all, good morning to you, sir, and thank you for coming to assist the Tribunal. I would, first of all, point out that, for reasons peculiar to yourself, you have, as an exception to the ordinary practices of the Tribunal, been afforded certain protective measures. And whereas your testimony can be heard by persons in the gallery, in other words, broadcast, your identity is concealed and your voice distorted so that no one who is listening in or watching the proceedings would be able to identify you, either by your face or by your voice. I would begin by reminding you that the solemn declaration that you took imposes upon the obligation to give truthful testimony under pain of the penalty for perjury, which this Tribunal is empowered to impose for misleading or untruthful testimony. The -- because of the protective measures that you have been afforded, I would, first of all, invite the Prosecution to ask the usher to hand you the pseudonym sheet, and if you are satisfied that it states your name and date of birth, if you would please sign it and hand it back to the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I sign it, here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please. And that is admitted under seal and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01700, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You have been called by the Prosecution, who sits to your right, and they have indicated that their examination of you would last for about two hours. Counsel for the accused, Mr. Stanisic, has indicated that their cross-examination may last for about three hours. And -- all of which means that your testimony will not be completed by the time the Court rises for the day at 1.45 in order to make the courtroom available for another trial. The sitting day is divided into segments of no longer than an hour and a half because the recording of the proceedings, the tapes that -- for the recording have to be changed at 90-minute intervals, and those breaks allow for the convenience and comfort of yourself as a witness and, indeed, everybody in and around the courtroom, including the Judges. But, if before the scheduled time for a break, and your testimony begins in the middle of today's proceedings, so the next scheduled break would in fact occur at about 12.05, if at any point before those breaks which are usually of 20 minutes' duration, you need to take a break, if you indicate it to us we will accommodate you. And if we might go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, when the conflict broke out in Zvornik, did you then move into Zvornik Town, to live there?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: We moved to Karakaj, in the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in what building did you live? Where did this building come from?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: We lived in -- in a factory called Famod. It was a clothes factory, also known as Alhos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just to clarify. I think you're referring here to the Serbian police. I'm asking about you personally. Did you have an apartment or a home that you moved into in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: That was later. When the war broke out, we were all accommodated in the Karakaj-based Famod, also known as Alhos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this apartment that you moved into later, who did it belong to before you moved in there and how did you come to be in possession of that apartment?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Those were Muslim apartments, and they were assigned to us for temporary use. When I say "us," I mean Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that apartment?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to move on now to ask you some questions about your knowledge of detention facilities in Zvornik. And, first of all, turning to around May 1992, do you recall if there was a detention facility operating in a location known as Ekonomija farm?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And also at that time, was there a building called the Ekonomija factory?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: There was a building, and there were barns for the cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The building you're talking about, was that a factory?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: No. That may have been the administrative building of the company that was known as Ekonomija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Since 1992, at this location known as Ekonomija farm, has a factory since been built there?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes. But that was only after the Dayton Accords. A factory of some sort, a food factory, a biscuit factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know who was held at this detention facility at Ekonomija farm?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Well, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know where they had been arrested before being taken to Ekonomija farm?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know where they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd just like to explore that just a little further. Do you know if they had been arrested in the Zvornik area or from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I believe that they were arrested in the territory of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know who guarded this facility?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The reserve police of the Zvornik police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to show a video now. This is 65 ter 3682. And I will be starting at 8 minutes into this particular video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise the building that we can see on the screen at the moment?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Which building is this?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: This is the building where people were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Is this the building at Ekonomija farm where people were detained?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And on the screen in front of you, you can see approximately three doors on the building. Which of these doors led to the room where detainees were held?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: At the first door to the left, looking from where I sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just for the record, this is at 8 minutes and 8 seconds into the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you describe the conditions of the room where the detainees were held?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The room was 4 to 5 metres wide. They had blankets. The toilet was outside. And that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to continue playing the clip now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: This is at 8 minutes and 40 seconds into the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the building that we've just been looking at?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: You can see a building with windows, and this is where the guards were billeted. This is where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this video now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01702, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, referring to May 1992, do you know who was in charge of the police guarding Ekonomija farm?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The entire police force?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps my question should have been clearer. Who was overseeing the guards at Ekonomija farm when it initially opened?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry, stop there. I think we need some redaction there, the reference to the relationship of this person to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, please, sir, I'm limiting this question to -- these following questions to the time that Milos Milanovic was in charge of the guards there, and if could you just limit your answers to that and we'll move into private session later on. Now, sir, how long did Milos Milanovic remain in charge of the guards at Ekonomija farm?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Approximately 20 days. 20 to 25 days, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you recall why he left or why he was relieved of that position?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I don't know why he left. I only know that he became sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you recall what, if anything, led to him becoming sick? What contributed to his illness or sickness?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I wouldn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if, at this time, I could attempt to refresh the witness's recollection about the circumstances of the person being spoken about becoming ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there any indication that the witness needs to have his memory refreshed, Mr. Dobbyn?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, he was asked if he recalled what if anything led to this particular person becoming ill and the question [sic] I see is, I wouldn't, no. I could try to explore that a little further with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see. It relates to that question, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. You remember the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I don't know if I've used the procedure in this courtroom yet, but I'll do my best. No, that's the problem we have here, Your Honour, is that this particular witness won't be able to read it because it's a transcript which we've only very recently received and it's in English. I can't direct him to the passage in B/C/S, so the only way I would be able to do it would be to read the passage to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the B/C/S version exists of all his testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S version does exist. The problem that as we've only recently received translations, I can't identify where the relevant B/C/S portion is, and in the interests of time I could simply read to him a small portion and see if that refreshes his recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honours. Now we are back to the -- to the situation that we had with two -- two witnesses before, and Your Honours ruled because Your Honours accepted that -- that that situation was different. Now we are back to the original situation when they have to refresh the memory of the witness. So Mr. Dobbyn can provide the -- the B/C/S version of the -- of the transcript of -- of -- of his testimony in the previous -- in other cases, and maybe the witness can -- can try to find the relevant passage during the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, I could refer to the page in the English version, and Defence counsel could direct us to where that is in the B/C/S version. That might take a shorter amount of time. And what I'm looking at is page 16 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What transcript are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. This is a transcript of an audio recording of a witness interview 22 June, 2005. The ERN is 0678-4042 to 4071. Actually, Your Honours I think we'll just move on. It is going to take a bit longer. And, if necessary, I will come back to it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, while Mr. Milanovic was in charge of the detainees at Celopek -- sorry, at Ekonomija farm, did you hear about any mistreatment of detainees under his charge?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could you tell us precisely what you heard.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I heard that paramilitaries came and beat one or two detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Who did you hear this information from?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I heard that from Petko Panic, the assistant commander, or perhaps from Slavko Eric, who was also an assistant commander. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll need a redaction there of the last line of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we could go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Again, sir, while answering my questions, please take care not to give away anything that could reveal your identity. Now, you have mentioned a detention facility at Karakaj Technical School. Was this facility also guarded by police?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same five men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were the detainees ever interrogated at Karakaj Technical School?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we please look at 65 ter 3419.17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the location on the picture in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I don't know which buildings you're referring to. This is Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you see the location where the detainees were held at Karakaj Technical School?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I would ask you to mark, if you can, on the picture, precisely where the detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: This was the entrance to the school work-shop. There was a door there. That's where the entrance was. And that's where the detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Just to make a bit more obvious, perhaps you could draw a larger arrow pointing to where the door is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suggest then that this be deleted and then an arrow be pointing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you. Could I tender this photograph now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. You asked the witness to circle the area where the detainees were held. The only thing that's on the photo so far is the arrow indicating the entrance. But in which part of that building were then the detainees held? Could you circle the part of the building, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. The circle that you have drawn shows that detainees were held only in a very small portion of that building. Is that -- that a correct reflection of your indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I made a mistake. There's a room on this side, and there's an entrance door, and there's a room underneath. I made a mistake when I did the drawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Perhaps if the usher could assist the witness to get the drawing right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Should it be a circle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, if you could. The -- the interest is to have you indicate where in this building the detainees were held and so if you can mark the area. If it is the entire building, then draw a circle around the entire building; if it is a smaller area of the building then, as precisely as you can, try and draw a circle around the part of the building where the detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Does that circle indicate the entrance, or does it indicate the entire area where detainees were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where the entrance was. I can't see very clearly, so I put on my glasses. Could I please do the marking again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. With the usher's assistance, let's try, for a third time, to see if you can indicate the part of the building -- Mr. Usher, would you please assist the witness. We're interested if you can circle the part of the building in which, to your knowledge, the detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll leave it to Mr. Dobbyn to complete this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, so now do we have the entire area where, from your recollection, the detainees were held in that building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Just quickly, can you describe, perhaps, the size of the room where the detainees were held?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The room was rather high. It might have been 5 metres by 5. And for the purposes of heat in the room, it was encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd seek to tender this photograph now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01703, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I believe it's time for the break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could Your Honours remain just a moment after the witness has left, just to raise scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've noticed we're doing a sort of -- an afternoon, morning, afternoon, morning week, but, of course, Karadzic isn't sitting and we've noticed that Courtroom I is available in the morning on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday and we were wondering whether that would be something that we could take advantage so we don't go morning, afternoon, morning, afternoon. And perhaps we can just raise that that so the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't think there is any dissent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the second matter is this: The estimate by the Stanisic team for Mr. Dobbyn's first witness this morning was three hours, not no cross-examination. The next witness, both witnesses who are here, there -- but the following witness who, on the face of it, might well be expected to start tomorrow, doesn't arrive until tonight and has to review four days of testimony, even though he is being called viva voce. So it seems highly improbable that we will be able to start with the next witness tomorrow, whether in the morning or the afternoon, because he is going to need all day, in which event, Your Honours, I was wondering whether -- I noted that Mr. Zecevic wanted time off to discuss exhumations. We could use, say, whichever it is, tomorrow morning or tomorrow afternoon to discuss that rather than taking another day next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zecevic has heard your suggestion, and, no doubt, we're all agreed that we'll see what productive use we can make of such time as is available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to come in, the Registry confirms the availability of Courtroom I tomorrow, so the -- we -- we could switch to morning sessions for the indicated times this week, beginning tomorrow -- when we resume tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off, we'd been discussing some detainees held at Karakaj Technical School. Can you tell us how long they were held at that location, those particular detainees?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: For about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Where were they taken to next?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: It was they moved to the misdemeanour court in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And under whose order were these prisoners moved?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: On the order of my superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, do you approximately recall how many witnesses [sic] we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than 15. Ten to 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, was this facility at the misdemeanour court also guarded by police?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes. They were the same guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Once the detainees were moved to the misdemeanour court, where did the guards who moved with them sleep?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: They were in the building of Novi Izvor, next to the misdemeanour court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now these two buildings, the misdemeanour court and Novi Izvor, are they joined to each other?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were non-Serbs also detained in the Novi Izvor building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Serbs or non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, who guarded that facility at the Novi Izvor building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: There were no detainees at Novi Izvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, perhaps if I can just explore this. I'd just asked whether non-Serbs were also detained at the Novi Izvor building; and you had responded that yes, they were. So can you clarify again, did there come a time when non-Serbs were also detained at the Novi Izvor building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: At that time, only the guards were accommodated in the building of Novi Izvor. At that time. I'm talking about the time when they moved from the technical school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: At some time after the detainees were moved from the technical school centre, did non-Serbs also come to be held at the Novi Izvor building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you saying at no time in 1992 non-Serbs were held at Novi Izvor, or was there sometime later on when they were?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Later. There were some later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was that non-Serbs came to be held at the Novi Izvor building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: That happened when people from Divic, that is, detainees from Divic, were moved to the misdemeanour court from Karakaj, and those who had been in the misdemeanour court were moved to the Novi Izvor building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time when there were detainees in the misdemeanour court and the Novi Izvor building, were the same guards guarding both locations?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: They were the same guards, and some others were brought in from the Zvornik police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So at that time were the misdemeanour court and the Novi Izvor building operating, effectively, as a single facility?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now before prisoners were placed in one of these facilities, were they first interviewed or processed somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: They were first processed by military security, after which they were brought to the Zvornik police station, and it was there that they were interviewed or interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And from there, were they then taken to one or other of these detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: After that, they were brought to Novi Izvor. Because there was more room there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to call up 65 ter 2288.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the building in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: This is the building of the Zvornik SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And is this the building you have just been talking about where people arrested would be processed before being sent to Novi Izvor?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this photograph now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01704, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on and look at another photograph now, and this is 65 ter number 3419.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise what's shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The SUP, the municipal building, the court-house, Novi Izvor, the misdemeanour court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, if we could perhaps mark these buildings. We will just wait for the usher to arrive, and then I'll tell you which buildings I'd like you to mark. First of all, could you put the number 1 over the misdemeanour court.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you put a number 2 over the Novi Izvor building.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes. Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, finally, could you put the number 3 over the Zvornik SJB building, the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this photograph with the markings, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the original version of the photograph, which is 65 ter 3419.20, shall be given exhibit number P01705, while the marked version shall be given exhibit number P01706. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we please move into private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, in 1992, were you aware of a group known as Gogic's Men?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What were Gogic's Men; and where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: They came from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Is Loznica in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Loznica is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And how would you characterise them? Were they -- were they some sort of a particular group; a unit, a military unit, paramilitary unit, or something else?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: They were a paramilitary unit made up of individuals with thick criminal records.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know how they came to be in Zvornik? Did they come of their own accord or did they come at someone's request?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: My assumption was that they had been brought by Chief Milos Pantelic, the chief of the Zvornik SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When they were in Zvornik, what uniforms, if any, did they wear?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
