utterances.text: They had wartime police-issue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were they involved in any criminal activity in Zvornik in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you know what sort of things they were doing? What sort of criminal activity were they engaged in?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Well, they stole stuff from shops, they broke into flats, they beat the police officers, they beat the Muslims. What else can you expect from people of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when they were removed from Zvornik; and, if so, when was that?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the date, but I do know that all the police force took their rifles, surrounded the building where they were, and we managed to chase them out, back to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And upon whose initiative were they removed?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I don't know at whose initiative. We just gathered together with our rifles, we surrounded this building, and we drove them across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you recall what the -- what the catalyst was for the police in Zvornik to remove them? Was there some particular thing that made the police want to remove Gogic's Men?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: It would happen that both the active and reserve police officers would be sent to take part in actions, in mopping up operations, into the trenches, et cetera; whereas, the Gogic's Men remained on their own in the town at a check-point. So practically they were on their own in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what was it about this that made the active and reserve police unhappy?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I said that they used to beat the police officers, that they stole things, that they killed Muslims, and lots of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we move into private session again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of a detention facility operating at the Celopek Dom Kulture building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know over what time-period this prison operated?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I don't remember. I believe that it operated in June and July, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Who guarded this facility?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Again, the reserve police from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know who was overseeing the guards at Celopek?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Cvjetko Jovic, a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did he hold any special position?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: He was just a reserve policeman, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Who was being held at Celopek Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: The locals of Divic. They had been taken to the separation line in Emnici Kalesija [phoen]. However, the other side didn't want them and they were returned by buses in the direction of Kladanj again on another separation line where they were again rejected by the other side. Then they were returned to Zvornik and they were put in the culture centre in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these people from Divic who were held at Celopek?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if the Celopek Dom Kulture building is still standing or looks the same today as it did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: Not the same as in 1992. I don't know what happened to it. It has been renovated, or maybe even extended, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now 65 ter 3419.82.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the photograph on the screen in front of you, are you able to pin-point the location where the Celopek Dom Kulture stood in 1992? And perhaps with the usher's assistance you could draw a circle around that location.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this photograph now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01707, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I think we need to move back into private session now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are already in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, sir, can you describe the condition of the detainees that came from Celopek Dom Kulture to the misdemeanour court.

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: A number of them had been wounded from fire-arms. We gave them a special room. We brought doctors in. They tended to their wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you recall if any of those people died after they were brought to the misdemeanour court building?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was any investigation into this incident at Celopek Dom Kulture ever initiated by the police?

utterances.speaker: ST-221
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, nothing happened in Zvornik. I believe that some -- that proceedings were initiated in Belgrade. I don't know whether they ever ended or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like now to call up a document. This is now P1696, marked for identification. It was used with the previous witness. What did I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The 65 ter is 2826. And could we please go to page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I discussed with -- with my learned friend about this document. Basically what is the situation? Your Honours, 65 ter 2826 is three documents. Three different documents. The -- the first page is one document. Let me ... let me briefly explain. The first page, with the ERN number 0057-7954 is the document by the Red Cross of Prijedor, of the municipality of Prijedor, dated 15th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could the usher show it to us, the first page, on the screen -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... page number 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 2826. And this document was sent to -- this is a request for approval of transit, sent to the Presidency of Republika Srpska in Pale, to Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic or Buha. And it's dated 15th October 1992, signed by the president of the Red Cross of Prijedor. So in the -- in the north-west Bosnia. Now the page 2 of the document is the list of the detainees, or the arrestees, and it's dated 24/09/1992. And it lists on -- on page 2 and page 3, it lists altogether 42 persons. Then page 4 is another list of the detainees, and this one has the -- has in the logo of the C -- SJB Zvornik, also dated 24th September 1992. And so does the fifth page, which is the list of -- of detainees dated 24 September 1992. Now, the last page of the document, page 6 -- or page 7, actually, the last page of the document, is another document, completely different document, dated 22nd of October, 1992, and it's issued by the Ministry of Justice and signed by -- by then-minister Momcilo Mandic, and it was directed to the municipalities of Hadzici and Ilidza. Now, Your Honours the situation is, therefore, the following: The first page of the document, of this 65 ter 2826, is one document; then, next four pages is the second document; and the last page is a third document. Nothing whatsoever connects these three documents. And to -- so, my suggestion is that that -- that -- that our friends from the Prosecutor should divide this into three documents, give them the appropriate 65 ter numbers, and only then use -- use this document as -- as a -- as a different 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what would be the -- the ERN number of the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The last one is ERN number 0057-7959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm afraid that is not the end. To make things even more complicated, I -- I talked to Mr. Dobbyn during the break, and I -- I thought that we -- that we have found an agreement on it. I say that these three pages, which are the list of the detainees, is a part of another document, which has already been admitted in the -- in the case file of -- in this -- in this case, and that is the document P393. If we can have the P393 on the -- on the -- on -- on monitor, please. Can we have the -- so the P393 is the document dated 22nd of October, 1992. It is the Republika Srpska Ministry of Justice, and this is a report sent to the president of the Presidency, to the president of Republika Srpska, the president of the Assembly, and the president of the government -- and the prime minister. Now, on page 3, Your Honours -- page 2 first. Page 2 first. It says: Information on the conditions in prisons and the -- and gathering -- gathering -- sorry -- collection camps of the war prisoners. And it says Zvornik under number 2. It is obviously the page 3 in English. So, on this very same page, in English, it says, the very last concerning Zvornik: "Enclosed herewith is a list of detained persons by category." And I say, Your Honours, that the previous document which we saw, 65 ter 2826, pages 2, 3, 4, and 5, are the part of this document and the list that is referred to in document P393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But -- but P393 does not contain the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I guess, Your Honours, it is the photocopying when these documents were seized, or when -- I don't really know when and how these documents were seized by -- by the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have, to be complete, 65 ter number of P393?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So what I would suggestion -- what my suggestion would be is that -- that -- that our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor actually upload again the -- the document P393, of course, with the leave of the Trial Chamber and with the agreement of the Office of the Prosecutor, including these -- these four pages from 65 ter 2826, and the first and the last page of that document should give them -- they should give another -- another numbers [sic] or one -- one other number -- one other 65 ter number so as to be separate documents. I'm sorry, it -- I -- I know it's -- it's pretty complicated, but I -- I think that -- that this would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and all involved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. And thank you for this, Mr. Zecevic. Now, are any of you - Defence or Prosecution - able then to say who authored this list? Was that the Red Cross or was it the SUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as the actual lists go, our understanding is that these were authored by the SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And as Mr. Zecevic has correctly said, the document at the front, which I believe is a Red Cross document, is completely unrelated to the list itself. I entirely agree with Mr. Zecevic's proposal. I had simply been -- I was going do get the evidence that was relevant to this document first and then deal with the suggestion but I'm happy to go along with what has been suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And mercifully, from my point of view, we are at the end of today's sitting. So overnight this could be sorted out and when we resume tomorrow we should have this sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we're about to take the adjournment for today. You, having been sworn as a witness, cannot have any communication with counsel from either side, and in such conversations as you may have with persons outside of the courtroom you cannot discuss your testimony. We are scheduled to resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning in another courtroom, to which you will be conducted. So if the blinds could be lowered and the witness can be escorted out and then we will rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is just one final matter also before we adjourn and that is that because there is no cross-examination of the last witness we didn't actually officially tender his 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that is now admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 92 ter -- the ICTY statement of witness 221, which is 65 ter 09119, shall be given exhibit number P01708, while the declaration, which is 65 ter 10576, shall be given exhibit number P01709. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dobbyn, could we before we adjourn today, extend a request to the Prosecution for an indication of the time the Prosecution is asking for the completion of the examination-in-chief of the remaining witnesses which are not witnesses called to comment on the adjudicated facts. Now, the Chamber's Senior Legal Officer has been through the file and has identified the following six witnesses for which we believe the Prosecution is asking time. It is ST-004; ST-097, that's Mr. Brown; it's ST-190; and then ST-219; 221; and 222, which we have heard today. All of these were added to the list on the 22nd of July. Now, so, we are speaking about four witnesses which we still need to hear, and the Chamber would like to know how much time do you need to have these witnesses taken through their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I'll get that information for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There could eventually be one more, which I'm not certain. That would be ST-041. ST-041, for whom a 92 bis motion is pending. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And we thank the interpreters and support staff for the extra ten minutes that we would have spent. And we resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
